summary:
RotationLab turns 45 years of NASA weather data into a practical comparison of four-year crop plans. It evaluates candidate rotations against 500 weather scenarios and shows farmers how each plan compares with what they grow today.

We checked the model in 14 US counties spanning all nine USDA ERS Farm Resource Regions. Across 22 mostly rainfed county–]crop checks, median correlation on held-out years was 0.42, reaching 0.87 for Nebraska corn. A correction fitted only on training data raised the median to 0.57 and reduced median held-out yield error from 0.89 to 0.52 tonnes per hectare.

On the app’s 300-acre Iowa example, the recommended rotation increased modeled average profit from USD 333 to USD 365 per acre annually. The suggested plan earned a rule-based Soil Health Score of 69, compared with 35 for the baseline. Farmers can then explore how changing rainfall or irrigation would affect their choice. The app clearly labels these results as modeled estimates and discloses its weaker performance in irrigated counties.
details:
The problem. Most farmers plan rotations the way they always have, while the rain and heat on their land are already moving. Rotations that build soil (legumes, cover crops, more crop variety) look risky when margins are thin. A farmer needs an answer for their own field, in dollars, with the point where that answer would flip.

What RotationLab does. A farmer types an address. In under a minute the app finds the county, the soil, the crops grown in recent years and the local prices and costs, and asks the farmer to confirm. From there it runs a full daily simulation of every feasible four-year rotation, with or without cover crops, through every real weather year since 1981. The output is three plans with the numbers that matter: average profit, profit in a bad year, water use, food produced and a 0 to 100 Soil Health Score based on USDA NRCS soil health principles.

Built on NASA data. NASA POWER daily weather drives everything: the water balance, the yields, the climate card that shows how this farm's rain, heat and season timing have shifted since 1981, and the tipping points. NASA GIBS layers (SMAP root-zone soil moisture and MODIS vegetation) put the farm in context on the map.

Transparent science, not a black box. The model uses the FAO-56 daily soil water balance and the FAO-33 crop response to water (with the values tabulated in FAO-66), the same published methods agronomists use. There is no neural network, so every number traces back to its inputs, and every value in the app is labeled Observed, Estimated, Your input or Assumption.

Tested against reality. We replayed the model on past weather in 14 counties covering all 9 USDA farm regions and scored it against USDA NASS county yields on the 8 most recent years, which the model never saw. In rainfed counties it follows the year-to-year swings in real yields, with a median correlation of 0.42 and up to 0.87 (Lancaster County, Nebraska corn) and 0.85 (Warren County, Kentucky corn). A light statistical correction raises the median to 0.57 and cuts the typical yield error by 42%, from 0.89 to 0.52 tonnes per hectare. Irrigated farms are the next step: there water is supplied rather than rained, and the current model does not follow those yields yet, so the app flags them clearly.

Decision tools beyond the plan. "What could change it" shows the rainfall, heat or water level where a different rotation wins. "What to check first" tells the farmer which single measurement (water supply or soil water capacity) is most worth getting before committing. Three climate settings (historical, recent years weighted double, trend continuing) let a farmer stress-test a plan.

Tools. Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy with Numba (the full simulation runs in seconds), Plotly, hosted on Railway. Code: https://github.com/I-Am-Money/Space-Apps-Rotation-Lab

Super Intelligence. The team directed AI coding assistants (Claude Code and OpenAI Codex), which wrote most of the code, tests and documentation. The team set the modeling rules, checked the results and approved every merge. An optional Claude explanation in the app is checked number by number against the results. No data, images or audio were generated by AI. In our 30-second video every view of the app is a real screen recording. The opening and closing farmland shots were generated with Higgsfield, an AI video tool, and carry a visible "SI-generated" watermark.
